title: The English break
hook: Henry VIII leaves Rome; Catholics and Protestants were both martyred in England

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther: grace, scripture, and an end to real wrongs. Your line was the abuses were real. Today the break crosses the sea. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

Thomas More had been the king's friend, and then his Lord Chancellor. Now he's in the Tower of London, and all he has to do to walk out is swear an oath. Others around him have sworn. His own family begs him to. He's a lawyer; he knows every way around a sentence. He won't swear it. And he won't say why. Today's title is the English break, and it is a story where faithful people died on both sides.
screen: `THE KING'S FRIEND, IN THE TOWER.` → `ONE OATH FROM FREEDOM.` → `HE WON'T SWEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the break. King Henry the Eighth wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon declared invalid. The pope would not grant it. So the king and Parliament cut the English Church off from Rome and named the king its supreme head on earth. Next, the cost to Catholics. Oaths were required, and refusing put a person in the king's prisons. Thomas More refused, and so did John Fisher, a bishop. Both were tried for treason and beheaded. More is remembered as saying on the scaffold that he died the king's good servant, but God's first. The Catholic Church honors both as saints. Then, the turn. Henry had sent some Protestants to the fire too, but under his daughter Mary, a Catholic who restored ties to Rome, Protestants were burned for heresy in far greater numbers. Among them was Thomas Cranmer, the archbishop behind the English Book of Common Prayer. Anglicans remember him and others as martyrs. Under the next queen, Elizabeth, it turned again: Catholic priests were hanged, among them the Jesuit Edmund Campion, whom the Catholic Church honors as a saint. Last, what both sides shared. The words of the apostles in Acts could be said of every one of them; in the Douay-Rheims they read, "We ought to obey God, rather than men." They disagreed about what God asked. They agreed it was worth dying for. Catholics and Anglicans today can honor their own martyrs without pretending the others weren't sincere. Martyrs on both sides.
screen: `THE KING CUTS TIES WITH ROME.` · `MORE AND FISHER BEHEADED.` · `UNDER MARY, PROTESTANTS BURNED.` · `UNDER ELIZABETH, PRIESTS HANGED.` · then, large: `MARTYRS ON BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for all who died for conscience, or, if you don't pray, remember them. Use the sit. Bring to mind a few names from today: Thomas More, John Fisher, Thomas Cranmer, Edmund Campion. Hold them side by side, not as teams. Then widen it, to anyone anywhere who has suffered for refusing to say what they didn't believe. If you pray, you can commend them all to God's mercy, the ones you agree with and the ones you don't. The bell holds the time.
Thomas More. The king's chancellor who refused the oath of supremacy and was beheaded, one of many who died on both sides of England's break with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: martyrs on both sides. Today, when you meet someone whose convictions cross yours, look first for the sincerity, and honor it out loud if you can. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps feast days for Saints Thomas More, John Fisher and the English martyrs; the Church of England also remembers its own martyrs of the period, and Catholics and Anglicans today meet in formal dialogue.

fork.setup: you're Thomas More in the Tower. one oath and you walk free. your family begs you. what do you do?
options: swear it, and keep your private reservations.
refuse the oath, and keep silent about your reasons.
escape by night to the continent.
fork.reveal: More refused and kept his reasons to himself as long as he could; he was beheaded, and the Church honors him as a saint.

trapdoor: what you thought: England left the Church because a king wanted a divorce.
what it means: the marriage case began the break, but the years that followed cost faithful lives on both sides.
what a scholar hears: More's careful silence before the oath of supremacy, and the reversals under Mary and Elizabeth.

notes: More's scaffold words are reported in a contemporary newsletter, paraphrased with 'is remembered as saying'.
'Others around him have sworn' replaces an earlier 'nearly everyone' (Fisher also refused).
Act of Supremacy wording 'supreme head on earth of the Church of England': confirm.
Cranmer 'wrote much of' the Book of Common Prayer; Anglican commemoration of Cranmer, Latimer and Ridley: confirm phrasing.
Campion hanged (hanged, drawn and quartered) under Elizabeth; canonized among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales: confirm.
Even-handed framing is deliberate per the index carry; confirm acceptable to a Catholic Keeper.
Editor: cut 'nearly everyone around him has sworn' and 'wrote much of' the Prayer Book as uncited; softened the claim about each martyr's last choice; fixed a garbled review note.
Editor 2: cut the uncited claim that each martyr 'stood on' Acts 5:29, now framed as words that fit them; varied the teach's closing line.

Audit: 'refusing was treason' corrected (refusing the oath of succession was misprision, punished by prison; More and Fisher were then tried for treason over the royal supremacy); 'now it was Protestants' corrected, since Henry also burned Protestants (e.g. Anne Askew, Robert Barnes). Confirm 'far greater numbers' under Mary is acceptable without a count.
